title: Notes on the Snow Mountain Verse
author: Zhanran (annotator)
excerpt: The Snow Mountain Verse comprises four lines within the Nirvana Sutra. When Sakyamuni Buddha, in a past life, was the young seeker of the Snow Mountain, he heard from the mouth of a raksasa the two lines 'All compounded things are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing,' and gave up his body and life in order to hear the remaining two lines ('When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescence is bliss'). Hence these four lines are called the Snow Mountain Verse.

inline.s: All compounded things are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing;
When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescence is bliss.

[The Snow Mountain Verse] The four lines found in the Nirvana Sutra. When Sakyamuni Buddha, in a past life, was the young seeker of the Snow Mountain, he heard from the mouth of a raksasa the two lines 'All compounded things are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing,' and gave up his body and life in order to hear the remaining two lines ('When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescence is bliss'). For this reason these four lines are called the Snow Mountain Verse.
The following passage is the World-Honored One, in the Mahaparinirvana Sutra, telling the Bodhisattva Kasyapa the story of how, in a former life, he gave up his body and life to obtain a half-verse.
Good man, in a past age, before the sun of the Buddha had risen
(the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world)

, I was then a brahmin, cultivating the bodhisattva path, and fully able to penetrate all the scriptures and treatises of the non-Buddhist schools. I practiced the path of quiescence and perfected all dignified deportment. My mind was pure and undefiled, not broken by any external thoughts that could give rise to desire. I extinguished the fire of anger and aversion, and upheld the teaching of permanence, bliss, self, and purity
(upholding the non-Buddhist teaching of permanence, bliss, self, and purity)

[Sun of the Buddha] A metaphor for how the Buddha can break through the darkness of delusion of sentient beings, just as the sun can dispel all darkness; it also signifies that the Buddha's Dharma is vast in compassion, saving all beings impartially and selflessly, like the sun shining over the whole earth.
[Dignified deportment]

The dignity and proper comportment that should be maintained in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. [Permanence, bliss, self, purity] The permanence, bliss, self, and purity spoken of here are not the four virtues of nirvana, but the four inverted views of ordinary beings (four kinds of inversion).
[Four inversions]

The world is a dharma of birth and death: impermanent, without bliss, without a self, and without purity; yet ordinary beings deludedly cling to them as permanent, blissful, a self, and pure, which is called the four inversions. [Four virtues] The four virtues possessed by the Mahayana Great Nirvana: permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Permanence: the essence of nirvana, eternally unchanging, without arising or ceasing. Bliss: the essence of nirvana, eternally quiescent, at ease, wholly possessed, without a trace of affliction. Self: the essence of nirvana, attaining great freedom, without the slightest bond. Purity: the essence of nirvana, freed from all defilement, utterly pure.
I searched everywhere for the Mahayana scriptures, yet had not even heard the name of the vaipulya
(yet had not even heard the name of the Mahayana scriptures)
. At that time I dwelt on the Snow Mountain. The mountain was pure and serene; flowing springs and bathing pools, groves of trees and medicinal herbs filled the land. Here and there among the rocks
(among the rocky ravines)
, clear streams flowed. Many fragrant flowers adorned it on every side. The birds and beasts were beyond reckoning, and sweet fruits flourished in profusion, whose kinds and varieties were countless
(whose kinds and varieties could not be numbered)

. There were also boundless lotus roots, sweet roots, and costus roots. At that time I dwelt alone within it, eating only the fruits. After eating, I bound my thoughts and sat in meditation. Through countless ages, I did not hear that a Tathagata had appeared in the world, nor the name of the Mahayana scriptures
(nor did I hear that a Buddha had appeared in the world, nor the name of the Mahayana scriptures)
[Vaipulya] The vaipulya sutras, a general name for the Mahayana scriptures.

Good man, while I was cultivating such difficult ascetic practices, the devas and gods led by Sakra, lord of the devas, were greatly astonished and gathered together. Speaking to one another, they recited this verse:
[Sakra (Shiti-huanyin)] The lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven, abbreviated as Sakra, lord of the devas, or Emperor Sakra.
All pointing one to another
(the devas were all pointing and discussing)
, in the pure Snow Mountain,
there dwelt a master quiescent and free of desire, a king adorned with merit,
who had left behind greed, anger, and pride, and forever cut off flattery and folly,
whose mouth had never spoken
(never once in his life had spoken)
harsh and coarse words.'
Then, in the assembly, there was a heavenly being named Joy, who also spoke a verse:
One thus free of desire, pure and ever diligent,
does he not seek the throne of Sakra, and the abodes of the devas?
(does he not seek the fruition of Sakra and the devas?)
If he were a non-Buddhist, practicing all kinds of ascetic penance,
then this man surely desires the very seat where Sakra dwells.'
Then another heavenly being, a sage-ascetic, spoke this verse to Sakra:
Lord of the devas, Kausika, you should not harbor this doubt,
non-Buddhists who practice ascetic penance, why should they seek the realm of Sakra?'

[Kausika (Jiaozhijia)] The clan name of Sakra. [Lord of the devas, Kausika, you should not harbor this doubt; non-Buddhists who practice ascetic penance, why should they seek the realm of Sakra?] Lord of the devas, Kausika, you should not harbor this doubt and think that this person is a non-Buddhist practicing ascetic penance. He practices all kinds of ascetic penance for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings; so why should he seek rebirth in heaven? [The realm of Sakra] The place where Sakra, lord of the devas, dwells, namely the Trayastrimsa heaven.

Having spoken this verse, he said further: 'Kausika, in this world there is a great being who, for the sake of sentient beings, does not covet his own body, and who, wishing to benefit all sentient beings, practices countless kinds of ascetic penance. Such a person, because he sees the faults within birth and death, even if he were to see
(if he were to see)

jewels filling this great earth, the mountains, and the seas, would have no greed or attachment for them, regarding them as spittle. Such a great being abandons wealth and jewels, his beloved wife and children, his head, eyes, marrow, and brain, his hands, feet, and limbs, his dwellings and buildings, elephants, horses, carriages, and his retinue of slaves and servants; and he does not even wish to be reborn in heaven, wishing only that all sentient beings may receive happiness. As I understand it, such a great being is pure and undefiled, all his fetters forever extinguished, desiring only anuttara samyaksambodhi
(only wishing to attain the fruit of Buddhahood)

[Fetters] 'Jie' (fetter) carries the meaning of knotting and of binding; it is an alternate name for the afflictions. Because afflictions knot together birth and death, they are called fetters; and because afflictions bind sentient beings and keep them from liberation, they too are called fetters. [Anuttara samyaksambodhi] The name of the Buddha's wisdom, translated into Chinese as 'supreme, right, and perfect enlightenment,' that is, the supreme wisdom that truly and equally realizes all truth.
Sakra, lord of the devas, said further: 'As you say, this person then takes upon himself all the sentient beings in the world
(this person, for the sake of drawing all sentient beings in the world out of suffering, practices ascetic penance)
. Great sage, if in this world there is a Bodhi tree that can remove the poisonous snake of affliction for all the devas, mortals, and asuras
(of)
, then if sentient beings dwell in the cool shade of that Bodhi tree, all the poisons of affliction are entirely extinguished. Great sage, if this person in a future age becomes a Sugata
(if this person becomes a Buddha in a future age)
, then we shall all certainly extinguish boundless blazing afflictions. Yet such a matter is truly hard to believe
(such a matter is truly hard to believe)
. Why? Countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who have aroused the mind of anuttara samyaksambodhi, upon encountering the slightest condition
(encountering the slightest condition)
, immediately waver from anuttara samyaksambodhi
(immediately turn back)

. Like the moon reflected in water: when the water moves, the reflection moves; like a painted image, hard to complete, easy to spoil. The bodhi mind is likewise just so: hard to arouse, easy to destroy.'

[Sugata] One of the ten epithets of the Tathagata. 'Su' means good, 'gata' means gone. The Buddha, having cultivated the right path and entered nirvana, goes toward a good destination; hence he is called Sugata, the Well-Gone One.

'Great sage, suppose there are many people who, armed with armor and weapons, firmly array themselves about to go attack bandits; yet when they face the battle line they are terrified and then scatter in retreat. Countless sentient beings are likewise. They arouse the bodhi mind and firmly array themselves; but seeing the faults of birth and death
(seeing the afflictions of birth and death)
, their minds are filled with terror, and they immediately scatter in retreat.
[Armor and weapons]
Armor and weapons.

'Great sage, I have seen that after these countless sentient beings arouse the mind, they all waver. Therefore, although I now see this person practicing ascetic penance, free of affliction and heat, dwelling on a perilous path, his conduct pure and clean, I cannot yet believe in him. I must now go and test him myself
(I will now personally go and test him)
, to learn whether he truly can bear up under the great, heavy burden of anuttara samyaksambodhi
(an old form of the particle meaning 'or not')

'Great sage, just as a cart with two wheels is able to carry a load, and a bird with two wings is fit for flight, so too is this ascetic. Although I have seen that he firmly upholds the precepts, I do not yet know whether he possesses deep wisdom. If he does possess deep wisdom, then I shall know that he is able to bear the great burden of anuttara samyaksambodhi.'

'Great sage, it is like a mother fish that bears many young, yet few reach maturity; like the amra tree, many blossoms but few fruits. Though the sentient beings who arouse the mind are countless, of those who reach attainment there are all too few to speak of.'

'Great sage, I shall go together with you to test him. Great sage, it is like genuine gold: only after it has been subjected to three tests do we know it to be true; namely, burning, hammering, and polishing
(the three tests for genuine gold are: burning, hammering, and polishing)
; and so it should likewise be in testing that ascetic.'

Then Sakra, lord of the devas, transformed his own body into the likeness of a raksasa of very fearful appearance, descended to the Snow Mountain, not far from him, and stood still. At that time the raksasa was fearless in heart, brave and mighty, hard to oppose, and his eloquence was orderly
(his speech was clear and orderly)
; and his voice was pure and refined, proclaiming the half-verse spoken by a Buddha of the past:
All compounded things are impermanent; they are the dharmas of arising and ceasing.'

[Raksasa] The general name for evil demons. [All compounded things are impermanent] 'Composed things' bears the meaning of ceaseless flux. 'All compounded things are impermanent' means that all things are in the midst of change (ceaseless flux). [All compounded things are impermanent; they are the dharmas of arising and ceasing] All things change and are impermanent; they are the dharmas of arising and ceasing. This is the cause of all suffering.
Having spoken this half-verse, he then stood in front of him, and the appearance he manifested was very dreadful; glancing all about, he gazed in every direction.
[Mian] To glance sideways out of the corner of the eye.
When the ascetic heard this half-verse, his heart was filled with joy. It was like a merchant
(a traveling trader)
, who on a perilous road, traveling at night and losing his companions, searches in fright
(seeking)
, and then suddenly meets his companions again
(suddenly encountering his companions)
, his heart filled with joy, leaping beyond measure; like one long ill who has not met a good physician to attend him and give good medicine
(who has not met a good physician to diagnose his illness and give good medicine)
, and afterward all of a sudden
(the same as
'cu'
, meaning 'suddenly')
he obtains it; like one drowning in the sea who all of a sudden
(the same as
encounters a boat; like a thirsty and exhausted person who meets clear, cool water; like one pursued by enemies
(like one pursued by foes)
, who is suddenly freed; like one long imprisoned
(like one long shut in prison)
, who all of a sudden
(the same as
hears that he may come out; and like a farmer who meets rain in a great drought; and like a traveler who at last returns home, and whose family, seeing him, is filled with great joy.
Good man, at that time when I heard this half-verse, the joy in my heart was likewise. Then I rose from my seat, and with my hand I lifted my hair
(pushing aside the long hair that covered my eyes)
, and gazing in all four directions I said: 'The verse I just heard; who spoke it?'
At that time I saw no other person, only the raksasa. So I said: 'Who has opened such a door of liberation? Who can thunder the sound of the Buddhas
(who can send forth the thunderous voice of the Buddhas)

? Who, amid the sleep of birth and death, alone awakens and proclaims such words? Who here can point out to beings starving in birth and death the taste of the supreme path? Countless beings sink in the sea of birth and death; who among them can act as the great helmsman? These beings are ever bound by the grave illness of affliction; who among them can be their good physician? By speaking this half-verse you have awakened my mind
(at last I understood the origin of all suffering)
, like the half moon, like a lotus that gradually unfolds
(like the half moon, like a lotus gradually opening)
Good man, at that time I saw nothing else, only the raksasa. Then I thought: 'Could it be this raksasa
(could it be this raksasa)
who spoke this verse?' I still harbored doubt: 'Perhaps it was not he who spoke it
(perhaps it was not he who spoke it)

. Why? This person's appearance is extremely fearsome. If anyone hearing these verses would have all fear and ugliness removed, how could this person, of such an appearance, be able to speak them? One should not find a lotus growing from fire, nor
(one should not)
cold water arising from the rays of the sun.'
Good man, at that time I thought again: 'I am now without wisdom
, yet this raksasa may have seen the Buddhas of the past and, from them, heard this half-verse; I should now ask him.' Then I went up to that raksasa
(so I went up to the very place where the raksasa was)
and spoke these words: 'Excellent, great being! Where did you obtain this half-verse spoken by the one of the past who is free of fear
(the Buddha)

? Great being, from where did you obtain such a half wish-fulfilling jewel? Great being, the meaning of this half-verse is the right path of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present. Innumerable sentient beings throughout the world are ever covered by the net of views, and for their whole lives within these non-Buddhist dharmas have from the outset
(ever)
heard the meaning of emptiness spoken by such a transcendent mighty one of the ten powers
(the Buddha)

[One free of fear] Another name for the Buddha. [Ten powers] The ten kinds of power possessed by the Tathagata: (1) the power of wisdom in knowing what is and is not the case; (2) the power of knowing the karmic retribution of the three times; (3) the power of knowing all the meditations, liberations, and samadhis; (4) the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties; (5) the power of knowing the various understandings; (6) the power of knowing the various realms; (7) the power of knowing the path that leads everywhere; (8) the power of the unobstructed celestial eye; (9) the power of knowing past lives without leakage; (10) the power of knowing the eternal severance of habitual tendencies. [Mighty one of the world] An alternate name for the Buddha. The Buddha is the most mighty and valiant in the world, having cut off all afflictions; hence he is called the mighty one of the world.
Good man, when I had asked this, he then answered me
(the raksasa then answered me)

: 'Great brahmin, you should not now ask me the meaning of this. Why? I have not eaten for many days now, and have sought everywhere without success. Distressed by hunger and thirst, my mind is confused; my words are not what I really intend
(my mind is confused by hunger and thirst, my words do not follow my heart, and I cannot answer the meaning of what you ask)
. Even if I now had the power to fly through the sky to Uttarakuru and even to the heavens, seeking food everywhere, I would not be able to obtain any. For this reason I speak these words.'
[Wu yu] To speak one against another, replying to each other. [Yudanyue] Uttarakuru, the northern continent.

Good man, I then said again to the raksasa: 'Great being, if you can speak this verse to me in full, I will be your disciple for the rest of my life. Great being, what you have spoken does not reach the end of its name, and its meaning too is not complete; for what reason do you not wish to speak it? The gift of wealth is exhausted, but the gift of Dharma is never exhausted. Although it has no end, it benefits many. Having now heard this half-verse of Dharma, my mind is stirred with wonder. May you now be so kind as to rid me of this doubt; speak this verse fully, and I will be your disciple for the rest of my life.'

The raksasa answered: 'Your wisdom is too great; you are only concerned for your own body, and do not see at all that I am now surely driven by hunger and suffering, so truly I cannot speak it.' I then asked him: 'What is it that you eat?' The raksasa answered: 'You need not ask. If I tell you, it will frighten many people!' I asked again: 'Here I dwell alone, and there is no other person. I do not fear you; why will you not speak?' The raksasa answered: 'What I eat is only the warm flesh of humans, and what I drink is only the hot blood of humans. Because my merit is thin, I can only eat such food, and I have sought everywhere in vain. Though there are many people in the world, they all have merit, and are also protected by the gods, and I have not the strength to kill them.'
Good man, I said again: 'You need only speak this half-verse in full
(you only need to complete the latter half of the verse)
; and when I have heard it, I shall offer and present this body to you. Great being, if I should die
(if I should die)

, this body would have no further use; it would be devoured by tigers, wolves, owls, and vultures, and yet I would not gain a fraction of merit. Now, for the sake of seeking anuttara samyaksambodhi, I abandon this insecure body to exchange it for a secure body.' The raksasa answered: 'Who would believe such words as yours? For the sake of eight characters
(for the sake of the eight characters of the latter half of the verse)
, you would abandon your cherished body
(you would abandon your cherished body)
[Chi-xiao]
The owl (
chi xiao
), also written 'chixiao', commonly called the cat-owl. The character chi is an ancient variant form of chi.

Good man, I then answered: 'You are truly without wisdom. It is like one who gives another an ordinary vessel and obtains a vessel of the seven jewels; so I, too, abandoning this insecure body, obtain the indestructible vajra body. As for your question of who will believe me, I have witnesses now: Brahma, lord of the great heaven, Sakra, lord of the devas, and the four great kings can attest to this matter. Further, bodhisattvas with the celestial eye, who for the sake of benefiting countless beings cultivate the Mahayana and possess the six perfections, can also verify it. And the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions who benefit sentient beings can also attest to me
(can also attest that I speak the truth)

: that for the sake of eight characters I give up my body and life.' The raksasa said again: 'If you are like this and can give up your body, then listen! Listen! I shall speak the remaining half-verse for you.'
[Brahma, lord of the great heaven] The lord of the first dhyana heaven.

Good man, at that time when I heard this, my heart was full of joy. I then removed the deerskin I was wearing, spread it as a Dharma seat for this raksasa, and said: 'Master, please take this seat.' Then I stood before him with hands pressed together, kneeling long, and said: 'I beg the master to speak the remaining half-verse for me well, so that it may be complete.' The raksasa then spoke:
[Heshang (upadhyaya)] The meaning of 'my teacher'; it is the respectful title used by monks for their personal teacher.
[Pressing the hands together]
The Indian gesture of reverence, also called the vajra-palm, which is to press the palms together and cross the fingers of both hands.
When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescence is bliss.'

The upper half-verse, 'All compounded things are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing,' is the cause of all suffering; the lower half-verse, 'When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescence is bliss,' is the path that ends suffering.

[When arising and ceasing have ceased] When the arising and ceasing of mental thoughts (including subtle thoughts) are entirely stilled, one realizes nirvana. [Quiescence is bliss] When the dream of ignorance ends, a peace and joy arising from within wells up, far surpassing the pleasures of the world (including those of kings, the very wealthy, and all who succeed and are happy), and there is no longer any of the world's anxiety, fear, or affliction.

Then, when the raksasa had spoken this verse, he said further: 'Bodhisattva-mahasattva, you have now heard the meaning of the complete verse; your wish is fully satisfied. If you truly wish to benefit sentient beings, then now give me your body
(at this time you should give your body to me)
Good man, at that time I deeply pondered this meaning
(deeply pondered the meaning of this verse)
. Then, on rocks and on walls
(on stones, on cliffs)
, on trees and on roads
(on trees, on the roads)
, I wrote down this verse. Then I retied my clothing, fearing that after death my body would be exposed, and I climbed up a tall tree.

Then the tree god asked me again: 'Excellent, good sir, what is it that you wish to do?' Good man, I answered: 'I wish to give up my body to repay the price of this verse.' The tree god asked: 'What benefit is there in such a verse?' I answered: 'These verses are the path of opening the wisdom of emptiness spoken by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present
(they are the path of opening the wisdom of emptiness and entering the gate of Dharma-light spoken by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present)

; for the sake of this Dharma I give up my body and life, not for offerings, fame, jewels, the wheel-turning sage king, the four great kings, Sakra, lord of the devas, Brahma, lord of the great heaven, or the pleasures of humans and gods, but for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings I give up this body.'

[Opening the path of the Dharma of emptiness] The path of opening the wisdom of emptiness, entering the gate of Dharma-light. [Gate of Dharma-light] Illuminating the phenomenal aspects of the dharmas and distinguishing their meanings is called Dharma-light; this Dharma-light is the gateway to entering the holy path, hence it is called a gate. The Bodhisattva's Necklace of Original Deeds Sutra says: 'For all sentient beings of the past, future, and present, open the path of the wisdom of emptiness and enter the gate of Dharma-light.' The Contemplation Sutra of Amitayus says: 'Possessing the hundred gates of Dharma-light, one enters the first ground.'

Good man, when I gave up my body, I said further: 'May all miserly and grudging people come and see me abandon this body. And may those who give even a little and become haughty also see that for the sake of one verse I give up this body and life as one would cast aside grass and wood.'
At that time, having spoken these words, I at once let go my body
(then immediately released my hands and feet)
, and threw myself from under the tree. Before I reached the ground, all kinds of sounds arose in the sky, and these sounds reached as far as the Akanistha heaven
(their sound rose to the heaven of the extremity of form)
. Then the raksasa resumed the body of Sakra
(the raksasa resumed the body of Sakra, lord of the devas)
, and caught my body in the air, setting it down on the ground.
[Akanistha] That is Akanistha, the heaven of the extremity of form.

Then Sakra, lord of the devas, and all the devas and gods, and Brahma, lord of the great heaven, bowed their heads and paid homage at my feet, praising me: 'Excellent! Excellent! You are truly a bodhisattva, able to greatly benefit countless sentient beings, wishing to light the great Dharma torch within the darkness of ignorance
(darkness)
. Because I cherish the great Dharma of the Tathagata
(because I cherish the great Dharma of the Tathagata)
, therefore I troubled you
(therefore I came to test you)
; and I beg you to hear me confess my fault! In the future you shall surely accomplish anuttara samyaksambodhi; I pray that I may be saved by you
(when you become a Buddha, you must surely save me)
.' Then Sakra, lord of the devas, and all the host of devas paid homage at my feet, took their leave, and suddenly vanished.
[Rao nao] To trouble, to annoy. [May I be saved] Praying to be saved. The character 'jian' (jiàn) is a grammatical particle indicating the passive, equivalent to 'be'.

Good man, as in the past for the sake of a half-verse I gave up this body, so by that cause and condition I was able to transcend fully twelve eons, attaining anuttara samyaksambodhi before Maitreya. Good man, the immeasurable merit I obtained all came from making offerings to the right Dharma of the Tathagata. Good man, you now likewise: having aroused the mind of anuttara samyaksambodhi, you have already surpassed immeasurable, boundless bodhisattvas, as many as the sands of the Ganges. Good man, this is called a bodhisattva abiding in the Mahayana Great Nirvana, cultivating the holy conduct.

[Mahaparinirvana] The Sanskrit 'mahaparinirvana,' whose meaning is: 'maha' means great, praising the virtue of stillness; 'pari' means entering, the meaning of going toward; 'nirvana' means extinction, the extinction of afflictions and of body and mind; 'na' means rest, the meaning of tranquil rest; combined they mean 'the great entering into extinction and rest.' Abbreviated as Mahaparinirvana, it refers to the Buddha's completing his work of saving the world and returning to perfect rest.
